about: 1P2 Structures is the 24-lecture structural mechanics course in Part IA of the Cambridge Engineering Tripos, given in weeks 1–8 of Michaelmas and Lent terms according to the 2025-26 syllabus page (the 2026-27 syllabus page could not be checked). Following that syllabus, it runs from external forces, friction and supports, through trusses, arches, thin-walled shells, cables, displacement diagrams and virtual work, to equilibrium, deflection and stresses of beams and the buckling of columns. It is examined in Paper 2 (Structures & materials), together with the 20-lecture Materials course; all Part IA students sit four three-hour written papers at the end of the year, each marked out of 200.
topics: External forces: equilibrium, friction and supports
Internal forces: trusses, arches and thin-walled shells
Cables and deflection of pin-jointed frames
Equilibrium of beams: shear force and bending moment

notes.h: External forces: equilibrium, friction and supports
notes.body:
The course opens with the forces applied to a structure from outside: the loads and the support reactions. Everything that follows (bar forces, bending moments, deflections, buckling) depends on getting these right, so the habit to build from the first lecture is a clear free-body diagram every time.

Forces, moments and couples
- A force has a magnitude, a direction and a line of action. Its moment about a point O is the force times the perpendicular distance from O to its line of action (in vector form, M = r × F).
- A couple is a pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces. It has zero resultant force, and its moment (force × separation) is the same about every point.
- Any set of forces in a plane can be replaced by a single resultant force acting along a suitable line, or, if the forces cancel, by a pure couple.

Equilibrium in two dimensions
- A body is in equilibrium when both the resultant force and the resultant moment are zero: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0 about any one point.
- That gives three independent equations for a plane body. Taking moments about a point through which unknown forces pass removes them from the equation, which is usually the quickest route.
- A two-force member (loaded at only two points) must carry equal and opposite forces along the line joining those points. If a body is in equilibrium under three non-parallel forces, their lines of action meet at a single point.

Distributed loads
- A distributed load w (force per unit length) can be replaced, for the equilibrium of the whole body, by its total (the area under the load diagram) acting through the centroid of that area.
- Uniform load w over a length L: resultant wL at L/2. Triangular load rising from 0 to w over L: resultant wL/2 at 2L/3 from the zero end.
- This replacement is fine for reactions but not for internal forces inside the loaded length: there you must cut the body and apply the idea to the piece you keep.

Friction
- In Coulomb's model the friction force F between two surfaces obeys F ≤ μN, where N is the normal force and μ the coefficient of friction. F = μN only when slip is about to occur (limiting friction).
- Equivalently, the total contact force must lie inside the friction cone of half-angle φ, where tan φ = μ.
- A block on a slope of angle α slides under its own weight once tan α > μ.
- Distributed friction: a rope wrapped round a fixed rough drum through an angle θ (in radians) can sustain a tension ratio of up to T₂/T₁ = e^(μθ). With μ = 0.3 and half a turn (θ = π) the ratio is e^(0.94) ≈ 2.57.

Supports
- Roller: one reaction, normal to the surface; free to rotate and to slide.
- Pin: a force in any direction (two components); free to rotate.
- Built-in (encastré): two force components and a moment.
- A plane body needs at least three suitably arranged reaction components to be held in place. With exactly three, and no mechanism, the reactions follow from equilibrium alone (statically determinate); with more, they do not.

Worked example
A simply supported beam AB of span 6 m carries 12 kN at 2 m from A. Moments about A: 6R_B = 12 × 2, so R_B = 4 kN. Vertical equilibrium: R_A = 12 − 4 = 8 kN. Check by moments about B: 6R_A = 12 × 4 = 48, so R_A = 8 kN.

Exam tips: show every reaction on the free-body diagram, pick the moment point that eliminates the most unknowns, and check the answer with a second, independent equilibrium equation.

notes.h: Internal forces: trusses, arches and thin-walled shells
notes.body:
Once the external forces are known, the next step is to find the forces inside the structure. The course does this first for structures that carry load mainly by axial force: pin-jointed trusses, arches and thin-walled shells.

Pin-jointed trusses
- Idealisation: bars joined by frictionless pins, loads applied only at the joints, self-weight ignored. Each bar is then a two-force member carrying only tension or compression along its axis.
- Counting rule for a plane truss with b bars, r reaction components and j joints: each joint gives two equilibrium equations, so b + r = 2j is needed for statical determinacy. If b + r < 2j the truss is a mechanism; if b + r > 2j it is statically indeterminate. The count is necessary but not sufficient: a badly arranged truss can satisfy it and still be a mechanism.
- Sign convention (one common convention, used throughout this pack): take tension as positive and draw every unknown bar force as tension. A negative answer then means compression.

Method of joints
- Resolve forces at a joint with no more than two unknown bar forces, then move on to the next joint.
- Zero-force members can often be spotted at once: at an unloaded joint with two non-collinear bars, both carry zero force; at an unloaded joint with three bars, two of them collinear, the third carries zero force.

Method of sections
- Cut through the truss (usually through no more than three bars of unknown force) and apply the three equilibrium equations to one side.
- Taking moments about the point where two of the cut bars meet gives the force in the third directly. This is the fastest way to find a single bar force in a long truss.

Symmetry and superposition
- A symmetric truss under symmetric load has symmetric bar forces, which halves the work.
- For small displacements and linear behaviour, bar forces from separate load cases can simply be added.

Worked example
A triangular truss has a pin at A and a roller at B, 4 m apart, with apex C 1.5 m above the midpoint of AB. A load of 30 kN acts downwards at C. By symmetry each reaction is 15 kN. Each sloping bar is √(2² + 1.5²) = 2.5 m long. At C, vertical equilibrium gives 2 × F × (1.5/2.5) = 30, so F = 25 kN in each of AC and BC, in compression. At A, the horizontal component of the force in AC is 25 × (2/2.5) = 20 kN, so the tie AB carries 20 kN tension.

Arches
- An arch carries load mainly in compression. A three-pinned arch is statically determinate: the extra hinge at the crown gives an extra equation (zero moment there).
- For a parabolic three-pinned arch of span L and rise h carrying w per unit horizontal length, moments about the crown for one half give H = wL²/(8h), and the arch is in pure compression because the parabola is the funicular shape for that load.
- For masonry, the useful idea (due to Heyman) is the line of thrust: if a line of thrust in equilibrium with the loads can be found that lies wholly within the masonry, the arch will stand.

Thin-walled shells under pressure
- In a thin cylinder (radius r, wall thickness t, internal pressure p), equilibrium of half the cylinder gives the hoop stress σ_θ = pr/t, and equilibrium of the end gives the axial stress σ_x = pr/(2t).
- A thin sphere has σ = pr/(2t) in every direction in the wall.
- Example: p = 2 MPa, r = 0.5 m, t = 10 mm gives a hoop stress of 100 MPa and an axial stress of 50 MPa.

Exam tips: state your sign convention, check the determinacy count before starting, and use a section cut whenever a question asks for only one or two bar forces.

notes.h: Cables and deflection of pin-jointed frames
notes.body:
This part of the course moves from forces to displacements. The two key ideas are compatibility (displacements and extensions must fit together geometrically) and the material law that links extensions to forces.

Cables
- A cable is idealised as perfectly flexible (no bending stiffness) and, in the first instance, inextensible. It can carry only tension, so it takes up whatever shape is needed to carry the load in pure tension: the funicular shape.
- Under concentrated loads the cable forms straight segments between the load points.
- Under vertical loads only, the horizontal component of tension, H, is the same at every point along the cable, since nothing else acts horizontally.
- For supports at the same level, taking moments for the part of the cable to one side of any point shows that H × sag(x) equals the bending moment at x in a simply supported beam of the same span carrying the same loads. This gives the shape quickly.
- With a load w per unit horizontal length the cable is a parabola. For span L and central sag d, H = wL²/(8d). The tension is largest at the supports: T = √(H² + (wL/2)²).
- Example: w = 2 kN/m, L = 40 m, d = 4 m. H = 2 × 1600/32 = 100 kN, the vertical reaction at each support is 40 kN, and the maximum tension is √(100² + 40²) ≈ 108 kN.
- A single point load P at midspan with sag d gives two straight segments and H = PL/(4d).
- Note the trade-off: a smaller sag gives a much larger tension.

Extensions of bars
- Strain ε = e/L and stress σ = T/A. For a linear elastic material, Hooke's law σ = Eε gives the bar extension e = TL/(EA).
- A temperature rise ΔT adds a free thermal extension αLΔT. A bar made too long or too short (lack of fit) contributes its error directly.
- In a statically determinate frame, thermal and lack-of-fit extensions cause displacements but no bar forces, because the frame can adjust freely.

Compatibility for small displacements
- If joints A and B move by small displacement vectors d_A and d_B, the extension of bar AB equals the component of the relative displacement along the bar: e = (d_B − d_A)·n̂, where n̂ is the unit vector from A to B.
- A movement perpendicular to a bar only rotates it and, to first order, does not change its length.

Displacement (Williot) diagrams
- Draw to a large scale, starting from a fixed point (a support).
- For each bar whose other end is known, draw its extension as a vector parallel to the bar (away from the known end for extension, towards it for shortening), then draw a line perpendicular to the bar from the end of that vector.
- Where two such perpendiculars from two different bars cross, you have the displacement of the joint they share. Repeat joint by joint.

Worked example
Joint C hangs from two bars, each of length L and axial stiffness EA, inclined at 45° to the horizontal and pinned to supports above. A load P acts downwards at C. Each bar carries tension P/√2 and extends by e = PL/(√2 EA). By symmetry C moves vertically by δ; the component of δ along each bar is δ cos 45°, so δ = √2 e = PL/(EA).

Exam tips: draw displacement diagrams large and label extensions with signs; in cable problems, always find H first.

Virtual work is one of the most powerful tools in the course. It links an equilibrium set of forces to a compatible set of displacements without needing a displacement diagram.

Real work
- When a load P is applied gradually to a linear elastic structure and its point of application moves δ in the direction of the load, the work done is ½Pδ (the area under the straight load–deflection line). This equals the strain energy stored.

The virtual work equation for a pin-jointed frame
- Take any set of external loads W and bar forces T that are in equilibrium (an equilibrium set).
- Take any set of small joint displacements δ and bar extensions e that are compatible (a compatible set).
- Then Σ W·δ = Σ T e, the sum on the left being over the loads and on the right over the bars.
- The two sets are completely independent. They need not come from the same loading, and the material need not be elastic. The only conditions are equilibrium for one set and small-displacement compatibility for the other.
- Derivation in outline: at each joint, the bar forces and external load sum to zero. Dot that zero sum with the joint's displacement and add over all joints. Each bar appears twice, once at each end, and the two terms combine into T × (component of relative displacement along the bar) = T e.

Finding a displacement: the unit load method
- To find the displacement of a joint in a chosen direction, apply a unit load there in that direction. Find the bar forces t_j it causes (any equilibrium set will do; in a determinate frame it is unique).
- Use the actual extensions e_j as the compatible set. The equation gives 1 × δ = Σ t_j e_j.
- The extensions can come from loading (e = TL/(EA)), temperature (αLΔT) or lack of fit, or any mixture.

Example
Joint C hangs from two bars of length L and stiffness EA at 45° to the horizontal, carrying P downwards. Real bar forces: P/√2 each, so e = PL/(√2 EA). A unit downward load at C gives t = 1/√2 in each bar. Then δ = 2 × (1/√2) × PL/(√2 EA) = PL/(EA), agreeing with the displacement diagram.
If instead one bar is heated so that it extends by e₁ = αLΔT, and the other is unchanged, the vertical movement of C is (1/√2) × e₁. No bar forces arise, since the frame is statically determinate.

Finding a bar force
- To find the force in one bar of a determinate frame, imagine that bar alone extending by a small amount while all others stay rigid. The frame becomes a mechanism; find the joint movements geometrically (this is the compatible set) and apply Σ W·δ = T e for the real loads.

Structural design
- Design is iterative: choose a layout, find the internal forces, size the members, check deflections, then adjust the layout and repeat.
- A tie sized at an allowable stress σ needs area A = T/σ, so its mass is ρTL/σ. A minimum-weight layout therefore tries to keep Σ|T|L small.
- Compression members also need a buckling check (see the last topic), so in practice they are sized more generously than ties carrying the same force.

Exam tips: tabulate bars with columns for length, t, T, e and t × e; get the signs of t and e consistent (tension and extension positive).

notes.h: Equilibrium of beams: shear force and bending moment
notes.body:
Beams carry load transverse to their length by bending. The first step is to find the internal forces at every section, using free bodies.

Internal forces at a section
- Cut the beam at a section and draw a free body of one side. To keep that piece in equilibrium, the cut face must carry an axial force, a shear force S and a bending moment M.
- Sign conventions vary between books, so always state yours. This pack uses one common convention throughout: bending moment positive when sagging (beam concave upwards), and S at a section equal to the net upward force on the part of the beam to the left of the section. Your lecture notes may use a different one; the physics is the same but signs in the formulae change.

Relations between load, shear force and bending moment
With a downward distributed load w per unit length and the convention above:
- dS/dx = −w and dM/dx = S.
- So the slope of the bending moment diagram equals the shear force, and M has a maximum or minimum where S = 0 (or changes sign, for example at a point load).
- A point load causes a step in the shear force diagram equal to the load, and a kink (change of slope) in the bending moment diagram.
- An applied couple causes a step in the bending moment diagram equal to the couple, with no change in shear force.
- Under a uniform load, S is linear and M is parabolic; with no distributed load, S is constant and M is linear.

Standard results worth knowing
- Simply supported span L, central point load W: reactions W/2, maximum M = WL/4 at midspan.
- Simply supported span L, uniform load w: reactions wL/2, maximum M = wL²/8 at midspan.
- Cantilever, end load W: maximum M = WL (hogging) at the built-in end.
- Cantilever, uniform load w: maximum M = wL²/2 (hogging) at the built-in end.

Worked example
A simply supported beam AB, span 6 m, carries a uniform load of 4 kN/m over its whole length and a point load of 12 kN at 2 m from A.
- Reactions: moments about A give 6R_B = 24 × 3 + 12 × 2 = 96, so R_B = 16 kN and R_A = 36 − 16 = 20 kN.
- Shear force: 20 kN just right of A, falling at 4 kN/m to 12 kN just left of the point load, stepping down to 0 just right of it, and falling to −16 kN at B (matching R_B).
- S changes sign at the point load, so the maximum bending moment is there: M = 20 × 2 − 4 × 2²/2 = 32 kNm (sagging).
- Note that adding the maximum moments of the two load cases separately (18 + 16 = 34 kNm) would be wrong, because they occur at different sections.

Statical indeterminacy
- For a plane beam, the degree of indeterminacy is the number of independent reaction components minus the three equilibrium equations (minus one for each internal hinge).
- A propped cantilever has four reaction components, so it is once indeterminate. A beam continuous over three simple supports is also once indeterminate. Such beams need compatibility (deflection) conditions as well, which the next topic provides.

Exam tips: draw the loading, SFD and BMD stacked vertically with x aligned, mark values at every change, and find the position of zero shear before computing the maximum moment.

Having found the bending moment, the next question is how much the beam bends. The link is curvature.

Curvature and bending moment
- Curvature κ is the rate of change of slope along the beam; for a circular arc κ = 1/R, where R is the radius of curvature.
- For a linear elastic beam, M = EIκ. The product EI is the flexural rigidity: E depends on the material and I (the second moment of area) on the shape of the cross-section.
- For small slopes, κ ≈ d²v/dx², where v is the deflection. With v measured upwards and sagging M positive (one common convention, used in this pack), EI d²v/dx² = M. With deflection y measured downwards instead, EI d²y/dx² = −M. Always state your convention.
- Curvature need not come only from load. A beam with temperature varying linearly through its depth h, by ΔT from bottom to top, has a free curvature κ = αΔT/h. Any such internal curvature can be integrated in the same way.

Deflection by integration
- Write M(x) from a free body, integrate once for the slope dv/dx and again for the deflection v, and fix the constants from the boundary conditions.
- Built-in end: v = 0 and dv/dx = 0. Simple support: v = 0 (and M = 0, so the slope is free).

Worked derivation: cantilever with end load
Let x run from the built-in end and, as is convenient for a cantilever, measure the deflection y downwards, so EI d²y/dx² = −M. The moment at x is hogging, M = −W(L − x) with sagging positive, so EI d²y/dx² = W(L − x). Integrating with y = dy/dx = 0 at x = 0:
- EI dy/dx = W(Lx − x²/2)
- EI y = W(Lx²/2 − x³/6)
At x = L: tip deflection WL³/(3EI) and tip slope WL²/(2EI).

Standard deflection coefficients
- Cantilever, end load W: δ = WL³/(3EI), θ = WL²/(2EI).
- Cantilever, uniform load w: δ = wL⁴/(8EI), θ = wL³/(6EI).
- Simply supported, central load W: δ = WL³/(48EI) at midspan; end slopes WL²/(16EI).
- Simply supported, uniform load w: δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI) at midspan; end slopes wL³/(24EI).
- Uniform curvature κ: cantilever tip κL²/2; simply supported midspan κL²/8.

Superposition
- Because the equations are linear, deflections from separate loads (and from internal curvature) add. Complicated cases can often be built from the standard coefficients.
- This also handles simple statically indeterminate beams. For a propped cantilever under uniform load w, remove the prop and require the upward tip deflection from the prop force R to cancel the downward deflection from the load: RL³/(3EI) = wL⁴/(8EI), so R = 3wL/8. The built-in end then carries 5wL/8.

Numerical example
A steel cantilever (E = 210 GPa, I = 8 × 10⁶ mm⁴) is 2 m long with 5 kN at its tip. EI = 210 × 10⁹ × 8 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.68 × 10⁶ N m². Tip deflection = 5000 × 2³/(3 × 1.68 × 10⁶) ≈ 7.9 mm.

Scaling
- Deflection under a point load grows as L³ and under a uniform load as L⁴, so doubling the span makes a big difference; deepening a rectangular section raises I as d³.

Exam tips: keep units consistent (N and mm, or N and m), state the sign convention, and look for a superposition shortcut before integrating.

The bending moment and shear force at a section produce stresses across it. This topic shows how to calculate them, which is what decides whether a beam is strong enough.

Engineer's theory of bending
- Assumptions: plane sections remain plane; the material is linear elastic with the same E in tension and compression; the section is symmetric about the plane of bending; slopes and strains are small.
- Strain varies linearly with distance y from the neutral axis: ε = y/R (y measured from the neutral axis).
- Result: σ/y = M/I = E/R. So σ = My/I, largest at the fibres furthest from the neutral axis.
- For pure bending there is no net axial force, which forces the neutral axis to pass through the centroid of the section.

Section properties
- Second moment of area I = ∫ y² dA about the neutral axis.
- Rectangle b × d (d in the plane of bending): I = bd³/12. Solid circle of diameter D: I = πD⁴/64.
- Parallel axis theorem: I about any axis = I about the parallel axis through the centroid + Ah², where h is the distance between the axes. Use it to build up T- and I-sections from rectangles.
- Elastic section modulus Z = I/y_max, so σ_max = M/Z. For a rectangle Z = bd²/6.
- Section tables list A, I and Z for standard rolled sections.

Worked example: T-section
Flange 100 × 20 mm on top of a web 20 × 100 mm (total depth 120 mm).
- Areas: 2000 mm² each. Centroids: flange at 110 mm, web at 50 mm above the base. Neutral axis: (2000 × 110 + 2000 × 50)/4000 = 80 mm above the base.
- I = [100 × 20³/12 + 2000 × 30²] + [20 × 100³/12 + 2000 × 30²] ≈ 5.33 × 10⁶ mm⁴.
- Under a sagging moment of 10 kNm: bottom fibre (y = 80 mm) σ = 10⁷ × 80/(5.33 × 10⁶) = 150 MPa tension; top fibre (y = 40 mm) 75 MPa compression.

Combined bending and axial force
- Superpose: σ = N/A ± My/I. An axial compression can cancel bending tension, which is the principle behind prestressing.

Composite beams and reinforced concrete
- For two materials bonded together, plane sections still remain plane, so strain is still linear, but stress jumps where E changes.
- Transformed section: replace material 2 by material 1 with its width multiplied by the modular ratio n = E₂/E₁. Find the neutral axis and I of the transformed section, apply σ = My/I, and multiply stresses in the transformed material by n.
- Reinforced concrete: concrete is assumed cracked and carrying no tension below the neutral axis. Transform the steel area A_s to m A_s of concrete (m = E_s/E_c). For a rectangular beam of width b with steel at depth d, the neutral axis depth x satisfies b x²/2 = m A_s (d − x).

Shear stresses
- The shear force produces shear stress τ = S A*ȳ*/(I b), where A*ȳ* is the first moment about the neutral axis of the part of the section beyond the level considered, and b is the width at that level.
- For a rectangle the distribution is parabolic: zero at the top and bottom, and a maximum of 1.5 S/(bd) at the neutral axis, i.e. 1.5 times the average.
- In I-sections almost all the shear is carried by the web, and almost all the bending by the flanges.

Exam tips: always find the neutral axis first, show the parallel-axis terms explicitly, and say which face is in tension.

A slender member in compression can fail by buckling sideways at a load far below the load that would crush it. This topic shows how to predict that load and how real columns are designed.

The Euler column
- Hypotheses: an initially perfectly straight, pin-ended, linear elastic strut, loaded exactly along its axis, with small deflections.
- If the strut deflects sideways by v(x), the axial load P has a lever arm v, so the bending moment is M = −Pv (with v upwards and sagging positive, the convention used for beams above). Then EI d²v/dx² = −Pv, i.e. d²v/dx² + k²v = 0 with k² = P/EI.
- General solution: v = A sin kx + B cos kx. The end conditions v(0) = 0 and v(L) = 0 give B = 0 and A sin kL = 0.
- A non-zero buckled shape needs sin kL = 0, so kL = nπ. The lowest load (n = 1) is the Euler load: P_E = π²EI/L².
- I must be the smallest second moment of area of the section (if the end conditions are the same in both planes), because the column buckles about its weakest axis.
- At P_E the deflection amplitude A is undetermined: the straight and slightly bent shapes are both in equilibrium.

End conditions and effective length
- In general P_cr = π²EI/L_e², where L_e is the effective length: the length of the equivalent pin-ended column (the distance between points of zero moment in the buckled shape).
- Pinned–pinned: L_e = L. Fixed–free (flagpole): L_e = 2L. Fixed–fixed: L_e = 0.5L. Fixed–pinned: L_e ≈ 0.7L.
- So changing pin-ended supports to fully fixed ones multiplies the buckling load by 4, and a cantilever column carries only a quarter of the pin-ended load.

Critical stress and slenderness
- Dividing by the area: σ_cr = π²E/λ², where λ = L_e/r is the slenderness ratio and r = √(I/A) is the radius of gyration.
- A short, stocky column fails by yielding at the squash load σ_y A instead. The two limits cross where π²E/λ² = σ_y, i.e. λ = π√(E/σ_y). For steel with E = 210 GPa and σ_y = 275 MPa this is about 87.
- Example: a solid steel rod 20 mm in diameter and 1 m long, pinned at both ends (E = 210 GPa). I = π × 20⁴/64 ≈ 7854 mm⁴, so P_E = π² × 210 000 × 7854/1000² ≈ 16.3 kN. Here r = D/4 = 5 mm and λ = 200, so σ_cr ≈ 52 MPa, well below yield: elastic buckling governs.

Imperfections
- Real columns are never perfectly straight or perfectly loaded. If a pin-ended strut has an initial bow of amplitude a (in the shape of the first buckling mode), the total amplitude under load P becomes a/(1 − P/P_E).
- The deflection, and with it the bending stress, grows rapidly as P approaches P_E. Yielding begins at the extreme fibre before P_E is reached, so real columns fail below both the Euler load and the squash load, especially at intermediate slenderness.

Column design
- Design curves (from tests and imperfection analyses) give an allowable stress as a function of slenderness, lying below both the yield and Euler limits.
- To improve a compression member: reduce its effective length (bracing, fixed ends) or increase I for the same area, for example by using a tube rather than a solid bar.

Exam tips: check which axis governs, state the effective length you are using and why, and compare σ_cr with σ_y to decide whether buckling or yielding controls.

cards.f: Couple
cards.b: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces. Its resultant force is zero and its moment (force × separation) is the same about every point.

cards.f: Equilibrium conditions for a plane body
cards.b: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0 about any one point: three independent equations.

cards.f: Resultant of a uniformly distributed load w over length L
cards.b: A single force wL acting at the midpoint of the loaded length (the centroid of the load diagram).

cards.f: Resultant of a triangular load rising from 0 to w over length L
cards.b: wL/2, acting at 2L/3 from the zero end (the centroid of the triangle).

cards.f: Coulomb friction
cards.b: Friction force F ≤ μN. Equality (F = μN) holds only when slip is impending, i.e. at limiting friction.

cards.f: Angle of friction φ
cards.b: The angle with tan φ = μ. At limiting friction the total contact force is inclined at φ to the normal; it can never lie outside this cone.

cards.f: Rope round a fixed rough drum (capstan)
cards.b: Maximum tension ratio T₂/T₁ = e^(μθ), where θ is the angle of wrap in radians.

cards.f: Reactions at a roller, a pin and a built-in support
cards.b: Roller: 1 (force normal to the surface). Pin: 2 (force components). Built-in (encastré): 3 (two force components and a moment).

cards.f: Assumptions for a pin-jointed truss
cards.b: Frictionless pin joints, loads applied only at joints, self-weight neglected. Each bar is then a two-force member carrying only axial tension or compression.

cards.f: Statical determinacy of a plane pin-jointed truss
cards.b: With b bars, r reaction components and j joints, b + r = 2j is needed; b + r < 2j means a mechanism and b + r > 2j means statically indeterminate. The count alone does not rule out a mechanism.

cards.f: Method of sections
cards.b: Cut through (usually) no more than three bars of unknown force and apply equilibrium to one side; moments about the meeting point of two cut bars give the third force directly.

cards.f: Zero-force members at an unloaded joint
cards.b: Two non-collinear bars only: both carry zero force. Three bars with two collinear: the third bar carries zero force.

cards.f: Hoop and axial stress in a thin cylinder
cards.b: Hoop σ_θ = pr/t; axial σ_x = pr/(2t), half the hoop stress (internal pressure p, radius r, wall thickness t).

cards.f: Wall stress in a thin sphere under internal pressure
cards.b: σ = pr/(2t) in every direction in the wall.

cards.f: Thrust in a three-pinned parabolic arch under uniform load
cards.b: H = wL²/(8h) for span L and rise h. The parabola is the funicular shape for load uniform per horizontal length, so the arch carries it in pure compression.

cards.f: Line-of-thrust (safe) idea for a masonry arch
cards.b: If a line of thrust in equilibrium with the loads can be found lying wholly within the masonry, the arch will stand (Heyman's safe theorem).

cards.f: Funicular shape
cards.b: The shape a perfectly flexible cable takes so that it carries a given load in pure tension. The same shape inverted is an arch that carries that load in pure compression.

cards.f: Cable under vertical loads only: what stays constant?
cards.b: The horizontal component of tension, H, is the same everywhere along the cable.

cards.f: Cable shape from a beam analogy (supports at the same level)
cards.b: H × sag(x) = bending moment at x in a simply supported beam of the same span carrying the same vertical loads.

cards.f: Cable with load w per unit horizontal length
cards.b: A parabola. For span L and central sag d: H = wL²/(8d), and maximum tension at the supports √(H² + (wL/2)²).

cards.f: Cable with a single central point load P
cards.b: Two straight segments; H = PL/(4d) for span L and sag d.

cards.f: Extension of a bar (elastic plus thermal)
cards.b: e = TL/(EA) + αLΔT.

cards.f: Small-displacement compatibility for a bar AB
cards.b: Extension = component of the relative displacement of the ends along the bar: e = (d_B − d_A)·n̂, with n̂ the unit vector from A to B.

cards.f: Displacement (Williot) diagram
cards.b: A scaled drawing of joint displacements: from a known point, draw each bar's extension parallel to the bar, then a perpendicular for its rotation; the crossing of two perpendiculars locates the joint.

cards.f: Virtual work equation for a pin-jointed frame
cards.b: Σ W·δ = Σ T e, where (W, T) is any equilibrium set and (δ, e) any compatible set of small displacements and extensions.

cards.f: Unit load method
cards.b: Apply a unit load at the joint in the direction wanted and find bar forces t_j; then the displacement δ = Σ t_j e_j, using the actual bar extensions.

cards.f: Do the two sets in virtual work have to be related?
cards.b: No. The equilibrium set and the compatible set may come from different situations; neither needs Hooke's law. Only equilibrium for one and small-displacement compatibility for the other.

cards.f: Thermal change in a statically determinate frame
cards.b: It causes displacements but no bar forces. Put e = αLΔT into δ = Σ t e to find the movement.

cards.f: Work done by a gradually applied load on a linear elastic structure
cards.b: ½Pδ: the area under the straight load–deflection line, equal to the stored strain energy.

cards.f: Mass of a tie sized at allowable stress σ
cards.b: A = T/σ, so mass = ρTL/σ. A minimum-weight layout aims to keep Σ|T|L small (with compression members also checked for buckling).

cards.f: Relations between w, S and M
cards.b: Using one common convention (sagging M positive, S = net upward force to the left of the section): dS/dx = −w and dM/dx = S. The slope of the BMD equals the shear force.

cards.f: Where does the maximum bending moment in a span occur?
cards.b: Where the shear force is zero or changes sign (for example under a point load), or else at a support or end.

cards.f: Effect of a point load on the SFD and BMD
cards.b: A step in the shear force equal to the load, and a kink (change of slope) in the bending moment diagram.

cards.f: Effect of an applied couple on the SFD and BMD
cards.b: A step in the bending moment equal to the couple; no change in the shear force.

cards.f: Maximum moment: simply supported span L with central point load W
cards.b: WL/4, at midspan.

cards.f: Maximum moment: simply supported span L with uniform load w
cards.b: wL²/8, at midspan.

cards.f: Maximum moment in a cantilever: end load W, or uniform load w
cards.b: WL, or wL²/2, both hogging and at the built-in end.

cards.f: Degree of statical indeterminacy of a propped cantilever
cards.b: One: four reaction components (three at the built-in end, one at the prop) against three equilibrium equations.

cards.f: Moment–curvature relation
cards.b: M = EIκ, where κ = 1/R is the curvature and EI is the flexural rigidity.

cards.f: Curvature for small slopes
cards.b: κ ≈ d²v/dx², so EI d²v/dx² = M (the sign depends on the conventions chosen for v and M).

cards.f: Cantilever with end load W: tip deflection and slope
cards.b: δ = WL³/(3EI); θ = WL²/(2EI).

cards.f: Cantilever with uniform load w: tip deflection and slope
cards.b: δ = wL⁴/(8EI); θ = wL³/(6EI).

cards.f: Simply supported beam, central point load W: midspan deflection
cards.b: WL³/(48EI).

cards.f: Simply supported beam, uniform load w: midspan deflection
Boundary conditions at a built-in end and a simple support
cards.b: Built-in: v = 0 and dv/dx = 0. Simple support: v = 0 and M = 0 (slope free).

cards.f: Free curvature from a temperature gradient
cards.b: A linear temperature difference ΔT across a depth h gives κ = αΔT/h.

cards.f: Engineer's theory of bending
cards.b: σ/y = M/I = E/R. Bending stress varies linearly with distance y from the neutral axis.

cards.f: Where is the neutral axis of a homogeneous elastic beam in bending?
cards.b: Through the centroid of the section, because zero net axial force requires the first moment of area about it to be zero.

cards.f: Second moment of area and section modulus of a rectangle b × d
cards.b: I = bd³/12 about the centroidal axis; Z = I/y_max = bd²/6.

cards.f: Parallel axis theorem
cards.b: I about any axis = I about the parallel centroidal axis + Ah², where h is the distance between the two axes.

cards.f: Combined axial force and bending
cards.b: σ = N/A ± My/I: superpose the uniform axial stress and the linear bending stress.

cards.f: Transformed section for a composite beam
cards.b: Replace material 2 by material 1 with widths multiplied by n = E₂/E₁; apply ordinary bending theory, then multiply stresses in the transformed material by n.

cards.f: Shear stress formula for a beam
cards.b: τ = S A*ȳ*/(I b): A*ȳ* is the first moment about the neutral axis of the area beyond the level considered; b is the width there.

cards.f: Maximum shear stress in a rectangular section
cards.b: 1.5 S/(bd), at the neutral axis; the distribution is parabolic, with zero shear stress at the top and bottom faces.

cards.f: Euler load for a pin-ended strut
cards.b: P_E = π²EI/L², using the least second moment of area I of the section.

cards.f: Effective lengths for common end conditions
cards.b: Pinned–pinned L; fixed–free 2L; fixed–fixed 0.5L; fixed–pinned about 0.7L.

cards.f: Slenderness ratio
cards.b: λ = L_e/r, where r = √(I/A) is the radius of gyration about the buckling axis.

cards.f: Euler critical stress
cards.b: σ_cr = π²E/λ².

cards.f: Slenderness at which Euler buckling and yield coincide
cards.b: λ = π√(E/σ_y); about 87 for E = 210 GPa and σ_y = 275 MPa.

cards.f: Effect of an initial bow on a pin-ended strut
cards.b: An initial bow of amplitude a grows to a/(1 − P/P_E), so bending stresses rise steeply near P_E and the strut fails below both P_E and the squash load.

cards.f: Which axis does a column buckle about?
cards.b: The axis with the largest effective slenderness L_e/r; with the same end conditions in both planes, the axis of least I.

questions.q: A block rests on a rough plane whose angle is slowly increased. If μ = 0.5, at about what angle does the block begin to slide?
questions.why: Sliding starts when tan α = μ, so α = arctan 0.5 ≈ 26.6°. 30° is arcsin 0.5 (using sin instead of tan); 63.4° is arctan 2 (inverting μ); 45° would need μ = 1.

questions.q: A simply supported beam of span 8 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 3 kN/m over the left-hand 4 m only. What is the reaction at the right-hand support?
questions.why: The load totals 3 × 4 = 12 kN acting 2 m from the left support. Moments about the left support: 8R = 12 × 2, so R = 3 kN (and the left reaction is 9 kN). 6 kN assumes the load is shared equally; 9 kN is the left reaction; 12 kN is the whole load.

questions.q: A rope passes over a fixed rough horizontal cylinder (μ = 0.25) with a total angle of wrap of 180°. One end carries a 100 kg mass. Taking g = 9.81 m/s², find the range of force that must be applied to the other end (pulling vertically downwards) to keep the mass at rest.
markScheme: Uses the capstan relation T_large/T_small = e^(μθ) with θ = π rad
Minimum force (mass about to descend): 981/2.19 ≈ 447 N
Maximum force (mass about to rise): 981 × 2.19 ≈ 2150 N; any force between these holds the mass
questions.modelAnswer:
The weight is W = 100 × 9.81 = 981 N. For a rope slipping (or about to slip) over a rough drum, the tension on the side towards which it tends to move is larger by the factor e^(μθ). Here θ = π and μ = 0.25, so e^(0.25π) = e^(0.785) ≈ 2.19.

If the pull P is small, the mass tends to descend, and the mass side is the tight side: 981 = P × 2.19, giving P ≈ 447 N.

If P is large, the mass tends to rise, and the pull side is the tight side: P = 981 × 2.19 ≈ 2150 N.

So the mass stays at rest for any force from about 447 N to about 2150 N.

questions.q: A plane pin-jointed truss has 9 joints and 15 bars and is supported by one pin and one roller. Which statement is correct?
options: It is three times statically indeterminate because of the supports
The necessary condition for statical determinacy, b + r = 2j, is satisfied
It must be a mechanism, because b < 2j
questions.why: A pin gives 2 reaction components and a roller 1, so r = 3 and b + r = 15 + 3 = 18 = 2 × 9. The counting condition for determinacy is met (it is still necessary to check the arrangement is not a mechanism). Comparing b alone with 2j ignores the reactions; it is neither once nor three times indeterminate, since b + r does not exceed 2j.

questions.q: A thin-walled cylindrical tank of radius 0.5 m and wall thickness 10 mm holds gas at 2 MPa. What is the hoop stress in the wall?
questions.why: Hoop stress σ = pr/t = 2 × 500/10 = 100 MPa. 50 MPa is the axial stress pr/(2t); 200 MPa uses the diameter instead of the radius; 25 MPa halves the axial stress again.

questions.q: A triangular pin-jointed truss is supported by a pin at A and a roller at B, with AB horizontal and 4 m long. Joint C is 1.5 m vertically above the midpoint of AB. A vertical load of 30 kN acts downwards at C. Find the reactions and the forces in all three bars, stating tension or compression.
markScheme: Reactions 15 kN upwards at A and B (by symmetry or moments)
Lengths AC = BC = 2.5 m, giving sin = 0.6 and cos = 0.8 for the sloping bars
Joint C: 2 × 0.6F = 30, so F = 25 kN in AC and BC
AC and BC are in compression
Joint A: horizontal equilibrium gives AB = 25 × 0.8 = 20 kN tension
questions.modelAnswer:
Taking moments about A, 4R_B = 30 × 2, so R_B = 15 kN, and vertically R_A = 15 kN. The pin at A has no horizontal reaction because the only load is vertical.

Each sloping bar has length √(2² + 1.5²) = 2.5 m, so the bar makes an angle with sin = 1.5/2.5 = 0.6 and cos = 2/2.5 = 0.8 to the horizontal.

At joint C, the horizontal components of the two bar forces cancel by symmetry, and the vertical components support the load: 2 × 0.6F = 30, so F = 25 kN. The bars push up on the joint, so AC and BC are in compression (25 kN each).

At joint A, the compressive bar AC pushes A outwards horizontally with 25 × 0.8 = 20 kN, so the tie AB must pull inwards with 20 kN: AB carries 20 kN tension. Vertical check at A: 25 × 0.6 = 15 kN, which matches the reaction.

questions.q: A cable spans 40 m between supports at the same level and carries 2 kN per metre of horizontal span. The central sag is 4 m. What is the horizontal component of tension?
questions.why: H = wL²/(8d) = 2 × 40²/(8 × 4) = 3200/32 = 100 kN. 50 kN and 200 kN come from using 16d or 4d in the denominator; 40 kN is the vertical reaction at each support (wL/2), not H.

questions.q: A steel bar 3 m long with cross-sectional area 500 mm² (E = 200 GPa) carries a tension of 50 kN. What is its extension?
questions.why: e = TL/(EA) = 50 000 × 3000/(200 000 × 500) = 1.5 mm (working in N, mm and N/mm²). 0.15 mm and 15 mm are factor-of-ten unit slips; 0.5 mm forgets to multiply by the 3 m length.

questions.q: A light cable spans 30 m between two supports at the same level and carries a single vertical load of 60 kN at midspan, where the sag is 3 m. Find the horizontal component of tension and the maximum tension, and describe the shape of the cable.
markScheme: Shape: two straight segments meeting at the load point
Vertical reaction 30 kN at each support by symmetry
Moments about the load point for one half: 30 × 15 = H × 3
H = 150 kN (or H = PL/(4d))
Maximum tension √(150² + 30²) ≈ 153 kN, constant along each straight segment
questions.modelAnswer:
With only a point load and no self-weight, the cable forms two straight segments meeting at the load.

By symmetry each support provides a vertical reaction of 30 kN. Take moments about the load point for the left half of the cable: the vertical reaction (30 kN) acts at a lever arm of 15 m, and H acts at a lever arm equal to the sag, 3 m. So 30 × 15 = 3H, giving H = 150 kN. (This is the standard result H = PL/(4d) = 60 × 30/12.)

The tension in each straight segment is constant, with components 150 kN horizontally and 30 kN vertically, so T = √(150² + 30²) = √23 400 ≈ 153 kN. This is both the tension in the cable and the maximum tension.

questions.q: Joint C hangs from two identical bars (length L, axial stiffness EA), each inclined at 45° to the horizontal and pinned to supports above, symmetrically placed. A load P acts vertically downwards at C. What is the vertical deflection of C?
questions.why: Each bar carries P/√2 and extends by PL/(√2 EA). A unit downward load at C gives t = 1/√2 in each bar, so δ = 2 × (1/√2) × PL/(√2 EA) = PL/(EA). PL/(√2 EA) is the extension of one bar, not the joint movement; PL/(2EA) and √2 PL/(EA) mishandle the cos 45° factors.

questions.q: Which statement about the virtual work equation Σ W·δ = Σ T e for a pin-jointed frame is correct?
options: The forces and displacements may come from entirely different situations, provided one set is in equilibrium and the other is compatible
It applies only if the material is linear elastic
The extensions e must be those produced by the loads W
It holds without change for large displacements
questions.why: The equation needs only an equilibrium set and a compatible set; they are independent, which is what makes the unit load method work. It does not depend on the material law, the extensions need not be caused by W, and the derivation assumes small displacements (so that bar directions do not change appreciably).

questions.q: Joint C is supported by two bars AC and BC, each 2 m long, inclined at 45° to the horizontal and pinned to supports A and B above C, symmetrically placed. With no load applied, bar AC is heated by 50 °C (α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C) while BC stays at its original temperature. Use virtual work to find the vertical movement of C, and explain why no bar forces arise.
markScheme: Free thermal extension of AC: e = αLΔT = 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 2000 × 50 = 1.2 mm; BC: e = 0
Unit vertical load at C gives t = 1/√2 in each bar (resolving at C)
Direction: downwards (extension of a bar in tension under the unit downward load)
Frame is statically determinate, so it accommodates the extension freely: no bar forces
questions.modelAnswer:
The heated bar extends freely by e = αLΔT = 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 2000 mm × 50 = 1.2 mm; BC has zero extension.

For the equilibrium set, apply a unit downward load at C. Resolving at C, each bar carries a tension t with 2t sin 45° = 1, so t = 1/√2.

Virtual work: 1 × δ = Σ t e = (1/√2)(1.2) + (1/√2)(0) ≈ 0.85 mm. The answer is positive, so C moves downwards by about 0.85 mm (it also moves sideways, which a horizontal unit load would give).

The frame has b + r = 2 + 4 = 6 = 2j (j = 3) and is statically determinate: the joint can move to accommodate any bar length change without any bar being forced, so the thermal extension produces displacement but no stress.

questions.q: A simply supported beam of span 6 m carries a uniform load of 4 kN/m over its whole length and a point load of 12 kN at 2 m from the left support. What is the maximum bending moment?
questions.why: Reactions: R_B = (24 × 3 + 12 × 2)/6 = 16 kN, R_A = 20 kN. The shear force falls to 12 kN just left of the point load and to 0 just right of it, so the maximum moment is there: 20 × 2 − 4 × 2²/2 = 32 kNm. 34 kNm adds the separate maxima (18 + 16), which occur at different sections; 18 kNm ignores the point load; 40 kNm ignores the distributed load to the left of the section.

questions.q: A straight beam is continuous over three simple supports (one pin and two rollers) and carries vertical loads. What is its degree of statical indeterminacy?
questions.why: There are four reaction components (two at the pin, one at each roller) and three equilibrium equations, so it is once statically indeterminate. 0 would apply with only two supports; 2 and 3 overcount the reactions.

questions.q: A cantilever 3 m long carries a uniformly distributed load of 5 kN/m along its whole length and a point load of 10 kN at its free end. Find the reactions at the built-in end and sketch the shear force and bending moment diagrams, giving the key values.
markScheme: Vertical reaction 10 + 5 × 3 = 25 kN
Fixing moment 10 × 3 + 5 × 3²/2 = 30 + 22.5 = 52.5 kNm (hogging)
SFD: magnitude 10 kN at the tip rising linearly to 25 kN at the root
BMD: zero at the tip, parabolic, reaching 52.5 kNm hogging at the root
Correct signs consistent with a stated convention
questions.modelAnswer:
Vertical equilibrium: the root reaction is 10 + 5 × 3 = 25 kN upwards.

Moments about the root: the point load contributes 10 × 3 = 30 kNm and the distributed load 15 kN × 1.5 m = 22.5 kNm, so the fixing moment is 52.5 kNm, hogging (tension on the top face).

Measuring s from the free end, the shear force magnitude is 10 + 5s kN: 10 kN just inside the tip, growing linearly to 25 kN at the root. The bending moment is M = −(10s + 2.5s²) kNm (negative, i.e. hogging, using the common sagging-positive convention): zero at the tip, curving parabolically to −52.5 kNm at the root. Its slope is steepest at the root, where the shear is largest, consistent with dM/dx = S.

questions.q: The length of a cantilever carrying an end point load is doubled, with the same load and cross-section. By what factor does the tip deflection change?
questions.why: Tip deflection is WL³/(3EI), so doubling L multiplies it by 2³ = 8. 4 is the factor for the tip slope (∝ L²); 16 is the factor for a uniformly distributed load of fixed intensity (∝ L⁴); 2 would mean deflection proportional to length.

questions.q: A propped cantilever of span L carries a uniform load w. What is the reaction at the prop?
questions.why: By superposition, the upward tip deflection from the prop must cancel the downward deflection from the load: RL³/(3EI) = wL⁴/(8EI), giving R = 3wL/8. 5wL/8 is the reaction at the built-in end; wL/2 would apply to a simply supported span; wL/8 is not a reaction here.

questions.q: A steel cantilever (E = 210 GPa, I = 8 × 10⁶ mm⁴) is 2 m long and carries a 5 kN load at its free end. Starting from M = EIκ, derive the tip deflection formula and evaluate the tip deflection and tip slope.
markScheme: Sets up EI d²y/dx² = W(L − x) with a stated sign convention
Integrates with y = dy/dx = 0 at the root to obtain EI y = W(Lx²/2 − x³/6)
Tip deflection WL³/(3EI) and slope WL²/(2EI)
EI = 1.68 × 10⁶ N m²
δ ≈ 7.9 mm and θ ≈ 0.0060 rad
questions.modelAnswer:
Take x from the built-in end and y downwards. The hogging moment at x is W(L − x), so EI d²y/dx² = W(L − x).

Integrate once: EI dy/dx = W(Lx − x²/2) + C₁, and C₁ = 0 because the slope is zero at the root. Integrate again: EI y = W(Lx²/2 − x³/6) + C₂, and C₂ = 0 because y = 0 at the root.

At x = L: EI y = W(L³/2 − L³/6) = WL³/3, so δ = WL³/(3EI); and EI dy/dx = WL²/2, so θ = WL²/(2EI).

Numbers: EI = 210 × 10⁹ × 8 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.68 × 10⁶ N m². δ = 5000 × 8/(3 × 1.68 × 10⁶) = 7.94 × 10⁻³ m ≈ 7.9 mm. θ = 5000 × 4/(2 × 1.68 × 10⁶) ≈ 5.95 × 10⁻³ rad.

questions.q: A rectangular beam 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep (bending about its stronger axis) carries a bending moment of 20 kNm. What is the maximum bending stress?
questions.why: Z = bd²/6 = 100 × 200²/6 ≈ 6.67 × 10⁵ mm³, so σ = 20 × 10⁶/6.67 × 10⁵ = 30 MPa. 60 MPa is the result for the beam laid flat (b and d swapped); 15 MPa uses twice the correct Z; 3.0 MPa is a factor-of-ten unit slip.

questions.q: A beam of solid rectangular section carries a shear force S. Where is the shear stress greatest, and how large is it compared with the average S/A?
options: At the neutral axis; 1.5 times the average
At the top and bottom faces; 1.5 times the average
Uniform over the depth; equal to the average
At the neutral axis; 2 times the average
questions.why: τ = S A*ȳ*/(I b) is parabolic over the depth: zero at the free top and bottom faces (where A*ȳ* = 0) and greatest at the neutral axis, where it equals 1.5 S/(bd). The faces carry zero shear stress, so the answer placing the maximum at the top and bottom faces is wrong; the distribution is not uniform; 2 times is incorrect for a rectangle.

questions.q: A T-section beam has a flange 100 mm wide × 20 mm thick on top of a web 20 mm thick × 100 mm deep. Find the height of the neutral axis above the base, the second moment of area, and the maximum tensile and compressive bending stresses under a sagging moment of 10 kNm.
markScheme: Neutral axis at the centroid: (2000 × 110 + 2000 × 50)/4000 = 80 mm above the base
Sagging: bottom in tension, σ = 10⁷ × 80/5.33 × 10⁶ ≈ 150 MPa
Top in compression, σ = 10⁷ × 40/5.33 × 10⁶ ≈ 75 MPa
questions.modelAnswer:
Neutral axis: both parts have area 2000 mm². The flange centroid is 110 mm above the base and the web centroid 50 mm, so ȳ = (2000 × 110 + 2000 × 50)/4000 = 80 mm above the base (40 mm below the top).

Second moment of area about the neutral axis, using the parallel axis theorem:
- Flange: 100 × 20³/12 + 2000 × (110 − 80)² = 66 667 + 1 800 000 ≈ 1.867 × 10⁶ mm⁴.
- Web: 20 × 100³/12 + 2000 × (80 − 50)² = 1 666 667 + 1 800 000 ≈ 3.467 × 10⁶ mm⁴.
- Total I ≈ 5.33 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

Stresses (M = 10 kNm = 10⁷ N mm): a sagging moment puts the bottom in tension and the top in compression. Bottom fibre, y = 80 mm: σ = 10⁷ × 80/(5.33 × 10⁶) = 150 MPa tension. Top fibre, y = 40 mm: σ = 75 MPa compression. The fibre further from the neutral axis (the bottom of the web) is the more highly stressed.

questions.q: The ends of a slender column are changed from pinned–pinned to fully fixed (fixed–fixed), with everything else the same. By what factor does the elastic buckling load change?
questions.why: The effective length halves (L to 0.5L) and P_cr ∝ 1/L_e², so the load rises by a factor of 4. × 2 forgets to square; × 0.25 has the effect reversed (it is the factor for going from pinned–pinned to fixed–free); × 8 has no basis.

questions.q: A solid steel rod of diameter 20 mm and length 1 m is pinned at both ends (E = 210 GPa). What is its Euler buckling load, approximately?
questions.why: I = π × 20⁴/64 ≈ 7854 mm⁴, so P_E = π² × 210 000 × 7854/1000² ≈ 16 300 N = 16.3 kN. 65.1 kN is the fixed–fixed value (× 4); 4.07 kN is the fixed–free value (effective length 2L); 1.63 kN is a factor-of-ten slip.

questions.q: Derive the Euler buckling load of a pin-ended strut of length L and flexural rigidity EI, stating your assumptions.
markScheme: Assumptions: initially straight, pin-ended, linear elastic, axially loaded, small deflections
Moment at a section M = −Pv, so EI v'' + Pv = 0 with k² = P/EI
General solution v = A sin kx + B cos kx
v(0) = 0 gives B = 0; v(L) = 0 gives A sin kL = 0
Non-trivial solution needs kL = nπ; lowest load P_E = π²EI/L²
questions.modelAnswer:
Assume a perfectly straight, pin-ended strut of linear elastic material, loaded exactly along its axis by P, with small deflections.

Suppose it deflects sideways by v(x). At a section, the axial load acts with a lever arm v, so the bending moment is M = −Pv (taking v upwards and sagging moments positive, one common convention). Using M = EI d²v/dx²: EI d²v/dx² + Pv = 0, or d²v/dx² + k²v = 0 with k² = P/EI.

The general solution is v = A sin kx + B cos kx. At x = 0, v = 0, so B = 0. At x = L, v = 0, so A sin kL = 0.

Either A = 0 (the straight shape, which is always in equilibrium) or sin kL = 0, which allows a bent equilibrium shape. That requires kL = nπ, so P = n²π²EI/L². The lowest such load (n = 1) is the Euler load P_E = π²EI/L², with buckled shape v = A sin(πx/L) of indeterminate amplitude.

questions.q:
A beam ABC is simply supported at A and B, with AB = 6 m, and overhangs B to a free end C, with BC = 2 m. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 10 kN/m on AB only, and a point load of 20 kN at C. The beam has a solid rectangular section 150 mm wide and 300 mm deep.
(a) Find the support reactions. [4]
(b) Sketch the shear force and bending moment diagrams, giving all key values, and find the maximum sagging and hogging bending moments. [8]
(c) Locate the point of contraflexure in AB. [3]
(d) Find the maximum bending stress and the maximum shear stress in the beam. [5]
markScheme: (b) SFD: +23.3 kN at A, linear to −36.7 kN just left of B; jumps to +20 kN at B, constant to C
(b) Zero shear at x = 23.3/10 ≈ 2.33 m; maximum sagging moment ≈ 27.2 kNm there
(b) Maximum hogging moment 40 kNm at B (20 × 2); BMD parabolic on AB, linear on BC
(c) M = 23.33x − 5x² = 0 gives x ≈ 4.67 m from A
(d) Z = bd²/6 = 2.25 × 10⁶ mm³; σ_max = 40 × 10⁶/2.25 × 10⁶ ≈ 17.8 MPa at B (tension on top)
(d) Maximum shear force 36.7 kN; τ_max = 1.5S/(bd) = 1.5 × 36 700/45 000 ≈ 1.22 MPa
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Reactions. The distributed load totals 10 × 6 = 60 kN acting 3 m from A. Moments about A: 6R_B = 60 × 3 + 20 × 8 = 180 + 160 = 340, so R_B = 56.7 kN (340/6). Vertical equilibrium: R_A = 60 + 20 − 56.7 = 23.3 kN (70/3). Check by moments about B: 6R_A = 60 × 3 − 20 × 2 = 140, so R_A = 23.3 kN.

(b) Shear force, using one common convention (S = net upward force to the left of the section; sagging moments positive). Just right of A, S = +23.3 kN. It falls at 10 kN/m to 23.3 − 60 = −36.7 kN just left of B. The reaction at B raises it by 56.7 kN to +20 kN, and it stays at +20 kN along BC (no distributed load there) until the 20 kN load at C brings it to zero.

Bending moment. On AB, M(x) = 23.33x − 5x². Shear is zero at x = 23.33/10 = 2.33 m, where M = 23.33 × 2.33 − 5 × 2.33² = 245/9 ≈ 27.2 kNm sagging: the maximum sagging moment. At B, M = 23.33 × 6 − 5 × 36 = 140 − 180 = −40 kNm, which agrees with taking moments of the overhang: −20 × 2 = −40 kNm. On BC the moment varies linearly from −40 kNm at B to zero at C. The maximum hogging moment is therefore 40 kNm at B. The BMD is a parabola on AB (zero at A, peak 27.2 kNm at 2.33 m, crossing zero, −40 kNm at B) and a straight line on BC.

(c) Point of contraflexure: M = 0 within AB when 23.33x − 5x² = 0, i.e. x = 23.33/5 = 4.67 m from A (14/3 m).

(d) Stresses. Z = bd²/6 = 150 × 300²/6 = 2.25 × 10⁶ mm³. The largest moment magnitude is 40 kNm at B, so σ_max = 40 × 10⁶/2.25 × 10⁶ ≈ 17.8 MPa, tensile on the top face and compressive on the bottom face over B. The largest shear force magnitude is 36.7 kN, just left of B. For a rectangle τ_max = 1.5S/(bd) = 1.5 × 36 700/(150 × 300) ≈ 1.22 MPa, at the neutral axis.

questions.q:
Joint C is supported by two pin-ended steel bars AC and BC, each 2 m long and inclined at 45° to the horizontal, pinned to rigid supports A and B above and on either side of C. Each bar has cross-sectional area 400 mm² and E = 200 GPa.
(a) A load P = 50 kN acts vertically downwards at C. Find the force in each bar. [3]
(b) Find the extension of each bar. [3]
(c) Use the virtual work (unit load) method to find the vertical deflection of C, and confirm it with a displacement diagram argument. [5]
(d) With no load, bar AC alone is heated by 40 °C (α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C). Find the vertical movement of C. [4]
(e) The load is now reversed to act upwards. If the bars are solid circular rods, check whether they would buckle, and find the largest upward load they could carry on the Euler criterion. [5]
markScheme: (a) Resolving at C: 2T sin 45° = P, T = P/√2 ≈ 35.4 kN tension in each bar
(c) Unit load gives t = 1/√2 per bar; δ = Σ t e = 2 × (1/√2) × 0.884 = 1.25 mm downwards (= PL/(EA))
(c) Displacement diagram: by symmetry C moves vertically, e = δ cos 45°, so δ = √2 e = 1.25 mm
(d) e = αLΔT = 0.96 mm in AC; δ = (1/√2) × 0.96 ≈ 0.68 mm downwards; no bar forces as the frame is determinate
(e) Bars now in compression of P/√2; d = √(4 × 400/π) ≈ 22.6 mm, I = A²/(4π) ≈ 12 700 mm⁴
(e) P_E = π²EI/L² ≈ 6.28 kN < 35.4 kN, so the bars would buckle; maximum upward P ≈ √2 × 6.28 ≈ 8.9 kN
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Bar forces. At C the horizontal components of the two bar forces cancel by symmetry. Vertically, 2T sin 45° = P, so T = P/√2 = 50/√2 = 35.4 kN, tension in both bars.

(b) Extensions. e = TL/(EA) = 35 355 × 2000/(200 000 × 400) = 0.884 mm in each bar (N, mm, N/mm² units).

(c) Vertical deflection by virtual work. Equilibrium set: a unit downward load at C gives t = 1/√2 in each bar. Compatible set: the actual extensions from (b). Then 1 × δ = Σ t e = 2 × (1/√2) × 0.884 = 1.25 mm, downwards. Symbolically δ = PL/(EA) = 50 000 × 2000/(200 000 × 400) = 1.25 mm.
Check by geometry: by symmetry C moves straight down by δ. The extension of each bar is the component of this movement along the bar, e = δ cos 45°, so δ = √2 × 0.884 = 1.25 mm, as before.

(d) Thermal movement. The free extension of AC is e = αLΔT = 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 2000 × 40 = 0.96 mm, and BC is unchanged. Using the same unit-load forces, δ = (1/√2) × 0.96 + (1/√2) × 0 ≈ 0.68 mm downwards. (In fact the two bars are at 90° to each other, so C simply moves 0.96 mm along the line of AC, away from A, while BC rotates about B; the vertical component is 0.96/√2.) The frame has 2 bars, 4 reaction components and 3 joints, so b + r = 6 = 2j: it is statically determinate, and the heating causes movement but no bar forces.

(e) Buckling check. With P upwards the bar forces reverse: each bar carries a compression of P/√2 = 35.4 kN when P = 50 kN. For a solid circular rod of area 400 mm², d = √(4 × 400/π) = 22.6 mm, and I = πd⁴/64 = A²/(4π) = 160 000/(4π) ≈ 12 700 mm⁴. Pin-ended, so L_e = L = 2000 mm: P_E = π² × 200 000 × 12 732/2000² ≈ 6280 N = 6.28 kN. The compression of 35.4 kN is far above this, so the bars would buckle. The largest upward load on the Euler criterion is P = √2 × P_E ≈ 8.9 kN, and a real design would need a margin below that for imperfections. A tube of the same area, or bracing to shorten the effective length, would greatly improve this.
